source_title: Connecticut's $410m plan to turn 125-acre power plant into park clears zoning
source_excerpt: For decades, a stretch of Norwalkâs waterfront was defined by smokestacks, industrial machinery and the imposing presence of a coal- and oil-burning power plant. Now, the same 125-acre peninsula overlooking Long Island Sound is poised for a radically different future. A $410 million investment from Connecticut couple Austin and Allison McChord is helping transform the former industrial site into Manresa Wilds, a public-facing destination built around open space, recreation and carefully managed cultural events.A major step for Manresa WildsAccording to the Hartford Courant and CT Mirror, Norwalkâs Planning and Zoning Commission unanimously approved a special zoning district covering the proposed Manresa Wilds development.The decision establishes the framework under which the McChords and their development team can continue refining plans for the site. The project is expected to combine parkland with amenities including walking trails, live music, private events, boat rentals and a restaurant or brewpub.The $410 million commitment includes the environmental remediation required to address the site's industrial legacy. However, the zoning decision does not represent the final approval for every element of the development. Future phases will require additional zoning reviews, detailed planning and traffic studies before construction can move forward.From industrial site to public destinationThe scale of the transformation is particularly striking because the property spent decades serving as a power-generation facility. The long-closed plant's buildings are now being incorporated into a broader vision that aims to give the waterfront a new public purpose.The first stage, known as the Northern Forest, is already under construction. As reported by the Hartford Courant and CT Mirror, the phase includes walking trails, open fields and outdoor classrooms and is expected to open next year.A later phase is expected to focus on the adaptive reuse of the former power plant's turbine hall and administration building. That portion of the project is currently targeted for completion in 2032.Community concerns reshape the plansThe redevelopment has not been without controversy. Nearby residents raised concerns about increased traffic, noise and the potential disruption caused by events at the site. More than 200 residents signed a petition opposing the proposed special zoning district and calling for a scaled-back approach.According to CT Mirror and the Hartford Courant, in response, the Manresa Wilds team conducted community meetings and collected more than 4,000 comments about the plans.Several changes followed. Plans for a hotel were removed, outdoor lighting was reduced and parking was capped at 200 spaces, with access managed through a reservation system.The approved zoning framework also places limits on events. No more than four monthly events can accommodate between 150 and 400 guests, while events drawing as many as 800 people will be restricted to four annually. On days when multiple activities take place, total attendance will be capped at 1,000.Preserving the past while opening the waterfrontThe project seeks to balance public access with the site's industrial heritage. Its redevelopment could eventually turn an inaccessible piece of Norwalk's waterfront into a destination combining nature, education, recreation and historic architecture.While concerns over traffic and neighborhood impact remain, the zoning approval marks a significant milestone.
